Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks : favicon arxiv.org 3 When comparing EfficientNetB3 and ConvNeXt, both architectures have their strengths and are suited for different scenarios in image classification tasks. Here’s a breakdown of their features and performance: - **EfficientNetB3**: This model is part of the EfficientNet family, which scales up the baseline model through a compound scaling method. EfficientNetB3 specifically has around 12 million parameters and achieves a good balance between performance and efficiency [1]. - **ConvNeXt**: This architecture is a modern adaptation of traditional convolutional networks, integrating concepts from transformer models. ConvNeXt aims to enhance the performance of convolutional networks by incorporating design elements that improve feature extraction and representation [5]. - **EfficientNetB3**: It achieves high accuracy, with a reported top-1 accuracy of around 83.5% on ImageNet, while being significantly smaller and faster than many other models [3]. - **ConvNeXt**: While specific accuracy metrics for ConvNeXt may vary, it is designed to outperform traditional CNNs by leveraging improved architectural concepts. - **EfficientNetB3**: Ideal for environments with limited computational resources and where speed is critical, such as mobile applications or real-time systems [10]. - **ConvNeXt**: Better suited for tasks that require high accuracy and can afford the additional computational overhead, making it a good choice for research applications or high-performance computing environments [2]. In conclusion, the choice between EfficientNetB3 and ConvNeXt should be based on the specific requirements of your project, including resource availability and the complexity of the tasks at hand. results.title: [Notes] Understanding ConvNeXt | Veritable Tech Blog
results.content: A new paper from Facebook AI Research — “A ConvNet for the 2020s”[2] — gradually and systematically “modernizes” a standard ResNet[3] toward the design of a vision Transformer. The result is a family of pure ConvNet models dubbed **ConvNeXt** that compete favorably with Transformers in terms of accuracy and scalability. Because ConvNeXt is borrowing designs from vision Transformers, the paper shows us how much progress in the vision Transformers can be explained by superior architectural design. Many of the new techniques introduced in vision Transformers that pushed the limit can also be applied to pure convolution networks. Personally, I feel particularly excited about this paper because it successfully replaced batch normalization with layer normalization without any loss of accuracy. Unfortunately, it is not widely adopted and most new ConvNet papers still use batch normalization in their released pretrained models. Hopefully, this layer normalization can stand the test of time and we can no longer be limited by the batch normalization for its degraded performance in small batch sizes. * RandAugment and random erasing: the `create_transform` helper function from timm is used. * ResNeXt-ify: use depthwise convolution and increase the network width. * Larger kernel size: use a 7x7 convolution instead 3x3 and move the convolution layer up ((b) to (c) in Fig 3). * Fewer normalization layers: from three to only one between the 7x7 and the 1x1 layers. * Substituting BN with LN: the Layer Normalization version perform slightly better. * Separate downsampling layers: the downsampling layer consists of a Layer Normalization and a 2x2 convolution with stride 2. Depthwise convolutions reduce the computation comparing to regular convolutions, but require the similar amount of memory to process the data. The performance of a model that heavily uses depthwise convolutions can become bound by memory bandwidth instead of computation capability. It is the main reason behind the slow speed of EfficientNet models[5] despite of their significantly lower FLOPs. The ConvNeXt models also use depthwise convolution extensively, so it is very nice to see that the paper compares the throughputs of ConvNext models and other popular models including RegNet, EfficientNet, DeiT, and Swin Transformers. results.title: ConvNext: The Return Of Convolution Networks - Augmented Startups
results.content: ###### The “Patchify” Layer In The Vision Transformer Architecture [3] ViT completely changed our fundamental approach to network architecture design. This enabled Swin Transformer to become the first Transformer model that was adopted as a generic vision backbone and achieved state-of-the-art performance across a range of computer vision tasks beyond image classification. ## Architecture & Approach The design process of ConvNeXt was driven by one key question: ### How do design decisions in Transformers impact ConvNets’ performance? The authors start with a standard ResNet (e.g. ResNet50) and gradually “*modernize*” the architecture to the construction of a hierarchical vision Transformer (e.g. Swin-T). ## **Macro Design** Swin Transformers follow ConvNets and use a multi-stage design, where each stage has a different feature map resolution. As there is a lot of redundancy in images, downsampling is a common standard for the stem cell in both Convolution Networks and Transformers. Vision Transformers have a more aggressive *“patchify”* strategy, which corresponds to a large kernel size (like 14 or 16) and non-overlapping convolution. Swin Transformers use a similar layer, but with a smaller patch size of 4 to accommodate the architecture’s multi-stage design. Despite the increased FLOPs for the depthwise convolution layer, the inverted bottleneck design reduces the whole ConvNeXt network **FLOPs to 4.6G**. ## **Larger Kernel Size** ###### Non-Local Self-Attention Block Beyond all that, the most differentiating aspect of vision Transformers is their non-local self-attention. ## Micro Design ConvNeXt also adopts some mirco scale architecture features from Transformers, i.e., layer level design aspects. ## Last Epoch ###### Plot of accuracies of different transformers and convolution architectures[1] On ImageNet-1K, ConvNeXt competes admiringly with two strong ConvNet baselines — RegNet and EfficientNet in terms of the accuracy-computation trade-off, and, the inference throughputs. ###### COCO object detection and segmentation results using Mask-RCNN and Cascade Mask-RCNN[1] Even on downstream tasks like object detection ConvNeXt based Mask R-CNN and Cascade Mask R-CNN achieves on-par or better performance than Swin Transformer. ## References [1] A ConvNet for the 2020s [2] Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows [3] An Image is Worth 16x16 Words [4] Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition #### Stay connected with news and updates!

results.title: LSTM vs GRU vs Transformer: What’s Best for Real-Time Driver Safety Prediction? | by Prince Kushwaha | Medium
results.content: # **LSTM vs GRU vs Transformer: What’s Best for Real-Time Driver Safety Prediction?**. Predicting driver safety in real-time is a complex challenge, especially when fusing multi-modal data like radar and human behavioral inputs. Choosing the right deep learning architecture is crucial to balancing **accuracy**, **speed**, and **resource usage**. In this blog, we compare the popular sequential models **LSTM**, **GRU**, and the attention-powered **Transformer**, focusing on performance, latency, and real-time feasibility. ## Why This Comparison Matters. For our driver safety prediction system, the architecture processes:. * **Radar input** via a CNN (LeNet). * **Human input** via YOLO + ResNet50. * Features fused with **Gated Attention**, then passed to a sequential model for final prediction. The decision now is: should we use **LSTM**, **GRU**, or switch to **Transformers**? ## Numerical Comparison Table. ## Visual Summary. *Image: Architectural difference in sequence processing.*. ## Real-Time Driver Safety Use Case. For applications like **live accident risk detection** or **driver drowsiness prediction**, latency and model size are critical. * **LSTM+Attention** or **GRU+Attention** provide a good balance between performance and efficiency. * **Transformers** can outperform in accuracy **only when you have large-scale data** and **powerful hardware** (e.g., GPU/TPU deployment). ## Final Verdict. Use Case Best Fit Small/medium dataset GRU or 1-layer LSTM High accuracy need Transformer Real-time systems GRU with Attention Long sequence handling Transformer. ## Pro Tip: Use Hybrid Approach. A common solution in recent research:. * Use **GRU with lightweight attention**. * Fuse radar and human inputs with **Gated Attention**. * If hardware allows, **switch to Transformer** in post-deployment optimization.
